scenario.speaker: dana
scenario.briefing:
This is the round where the Neo Smart Living engagement becomes quantitative. The focus groups told us *why* homeowners hesitate — privacy, climate comfort, and above all price. Now the board needs numbers that project: how many qualified homeowners would buy the Tahoe Mini, at what price, positioned around which concept.

Two deliverables today.

**First, the survey instrument.** Marcus assembled a question bank from our discussion guide and the focus-group findings; you select what makes the final questionnaire. Remember what you practiced on the TrailTonic favor — the funnel, the wording discipline, demographics that answer to objectives. This one is longer and higher-stakes: screener, concept reactions, an open end, pricing, demographics.

**Second, the sample size.** Neo's board wants to choose their own precision level, so I'm presenting three options at three price points of accuracy. You compute all three. Marcus's memo walks through the formula; the z-table and the finite-population correction are in the Guides, and the population count you need is in the Resources.

Work backward from the decision, as always: every question and every respondent we buy has to earn its place in front of that board.

— Dana

inbox.subject: Neo moves to the quantitative phase
inbox.body:
The qualitative phase is wrapped and the client is happy — now we cash it in. Everything we heard in the focus groups becomes a hypothesis the survey must test at scale: is cost really the top barrier? Do the wellness and home-office concepts hold up beyond thirty-two people in a room? Where does $23,000 sit against what homeowners will actually pay?

Your survey build is the instrument that answers those questions. Choose from Marcus's question bank, and hold every item to the standard you used on the TrailTonic favor.

On sampling: Neo's board is more involved than most clients — they want to *choose* how much precision to buy. So I'm presenting three sample-size options side by side: a board-presentation standard, a regulatory-grade option (their counsel asked, don't ask me why), and a segment-analysis standard that keeps the subgroup cuts stable. You compute all three; I'll do the talking.

The qualified-population figure you need is in the Resources — the housing atlas extract puts N at 300,000 households. Use the conservative p = 0.5, apply the finite-population correction, and round up. A fraction of a respondent has never answered a survey.

— Dana

inbox.subject: Sample-size math — the five-minute version
inbox.body:
Before you touch the three estimates, here's the whole procedure. Two steps, no shortcuts skipped.

**Step 1 — base sample size (infinite population):**

n0 = z² · p(1−p) / e²

where z comes from the confidence level (see the z-table in the Guides), p = 0.5 unless you know better (you don't — 0.5 is the conservative maximum), and e is the margin of error *as a decimal*. ±5% means e = 0.05, not 5.

**Step 2 — finite-population correction (FPC):**

n = n0 / (1 + (n0 − 1) / N)

where N is the size of the population you're sampling from. When N is known and finite, the correction trims the required sample — skipping it overstates what the client must buy.

**Worked example (numbers deliberately not the ones you need):** say 90% confidence (z = 1.645), ±5% margin, N = 50,000.

- n0 = 1.645² · 0.25 / 0.05² = 2.706 · 0.25 / 0.0025 ≈ 270.6
- n = 270.6 / (1 + 269.6 / 50,000) = 270.6 / 1.0054 ≈ 269.2
- Round UP: **270 respondents.**

Run your three the same way: z from the table, e as a decimal, p = 0.5, FPC with N = 300,000, round up. Show Dana whole respondents.

— Marcus

pages.title: Build Neo Smart Living's Product Survey
pages.intro:
Assemble the questionnaire section by section from Marcus's question bank. Respondents will read a description of the **Tahoe Mini** — a 117 sq ft factory-built backyard unit, delivered and installed for $23,000, pre-wired, with smart entry and floor-to-ceiling dual-pane glass — before the concept-reaction questions. Every question you keep should trace to a decision Neo has to make.

*Note: alongside the sections you assemble here, the instrument carries a fixed stated-primary-use item ("If you were to install a Tahoe Mini, what would be its primary use?" with an Other — please specify open end) that Neo requested verbatim.*

pages.title: Estimate the Sample Size — Three Options for Neo's Board

tasks.title: Neo Smart Living Product Survey
tasks.prompt: Build the final instrument: one introduction, two screener questions, three concept-reaction questions (asked after respondents read the Tahoe Mini description), one open-ended question, three pricing questions, and eight demographic questions.

sections.label: Survey Introduction
sections.note: Select the 1 introduction that follows best practice.

options.label: Neutral introduction with purpose, length, and anonymity
options.text: Thank you for participating. We are an independent research firm conducting a joint study with a Southern California home-products company about how homeowners use and improve their outdoor space. The survey takes about 8–10 minutes. Your responses are anonymous and will be reported only in aggregate. There are no right or wrong answers — we want your candid opinions — and you may skip any question or exit at any time.

options.label: Product-hype introduction
options.text: Get ready to see the future of backyard living! The revolutionary Tahoe Mini is changing how Southern California works, rests, and plays — and we can't wait to hear how excited you are. Let's go!

options.label: Curt instruction-only introduction
options.text: This survey is about backyard structures. Complete every question in order. Estimated time: unknown.

sections.label: Screener
sections.note: 2 questions that qualify the right respondents.

options.label: Home-ownership and yard screen
options.text: Which best describes your current housing situation?
choices: I own and live in a single-family home with usable backyard space
I own and live in a single-family home without usable yard space
I own a condo or townhome

options.label: Prior consideration of backyard units
options.text: Before today, had you ever considered adding a standalone structure — a studio, office, or finished shed — to your backyard?
choices: Yes — I researched options or requested quotes
Yes — I thought about it but took no action
No — I had never considered it

options.label: Junk qualifier
options.text: Do you like houses?

options.label: Quota-revealing screen
options.text: This study is only for homeowners with large backyards who are excited about innovative new backyard products. Are you one of them?

sections.label: Concept Reactions
sections.note: After the Tahoe Mini description, 3 reaction questions.

options.label: Purchase interest at the stated price (1–5)
options.text: Based on the description you just read, how interested would you be in purchasing the Tahoe Mini at $23,000, delivered and installed?

options.label: Purchase likelihood within 24 months (1–5)
options.text: How likely are you to purchase a backyard unit like the Tahoe Mini within the next 24 months?

options.label: Concept-appeal matrix across five positionings (1–5)
options.text: How appealing is each of the following ways of using the Tahoe Mini? Rate each from 1 (not at all appealing) to 5 (extremely appealing).

options.label: Flat yes/no purchase question
options.text: Would you buy the Tahoe Mini?

options.label: Leading superlative item
options.text: How impressed are you by the Tahoe Mini's stunning design and unbeatable value?

options.label: Unpriced interest item (duplicate)
options.text: How interested are you in purchasing the Tahoe Mini?

sections.label: Open-Ended Question
sections.note: Select the 1 open-ended question that will surface barriers in respondents' own words.

options.label: Concerns that reduce purchase likelihood
options.text: What concerns, if any, would reduce your likelihood of purchasing the Tahoe Mini? Please be as specific as you can.

options.label: Tell us anything
options.text: Tell us anything.

options.label: Three things you love
options.text: List three things you love about the Tahoe Mini.

options.label: Too-expensive threshold
options.text: At what price would a unit like the Tahoe Mini be so expensive that you would not consider purchasing it? Please enter a dollar amount.

options.label: Bargain threshold
options.text: At what price would a unit like the Tahoe Mini be a bargain — a great purchase for the money? Please enter a dollar amount.

options.label: Purchase-likelihood ladder at three price points
options.text: For each price below, what is the likelihood (from 0% to 100%) that you would purchase the Tahoe Mini at that price?

options.label: Is the price fair? (yes/no)
options.text: Is $23,000 a fair price for the Tahoe Mini?

options.label: Blunt income question (misplaced)
options.text: How much money do you make?

options.label: Open-ended ideal price
options.text: In your view, what should a unit like the Tahoe Mini cost? Please enter a dollar amount.

tasks.title: Sample-Size Estimates for Neo's Board
tasks.prompt: Dana is presenting three precision standards to Neo's board. Compute the required sample size for each, using n0 = z² · p(1−p) / e² followed by the finite-population correction n = n0 / (1 + (n0 − 1) / N). The z-table is in the Guides; the qualified population count comes from the SoCal Housing & Lot-Use Atlas extract in the Resources.

entries.label: Estimate 1 — Board-presentation standard
entries.context: **Board-presentation standard: 95% confidence, ±3.1% margin of error.** Target population N = 300,000 qualified households (SoCal Housing & Lot-Use Atlas). Use p = 0.5, apply the finite-population correction, and round up to a whole respondent.

entries.label: Estimate 2 — Regulatory-grade precision
entries.context: **Regulatory-grade precision: 99% confidence, ±1.0% margin of error.** Target population N = 300,000 qualified households (SoCal Housing & Lot-Use Atlas). Use p = 0.5, apply the finite-population correction, and round up to a whole respondent.

entries.label: Estimate 3 — Segment-analysis standard
entries.context: **Segment-analysis standard: 95% confidence, ±2.4% margin of error.** Target population N = 300,000 qualified households (SoCal Housing & Lot-Use Atlas). Use p = 0.5, apply the finite-population correction, and round up to a whole respondent.

guides.title: Survey-Building Fundamentals
guides.body:
**Structure the questionnaire as a funnel** — broad and easy at the top, specific and personal at the bottom:

1. **Introduction & consent.** State the purpose neutrally, give an honest length estimate, promise anonymity, note there are no right or wrong answers, and allow skipping or exiting. An introduction that sells the product corrupts every response after it.
2. **Screener.** Qualify respondents against the target-population definition before they invest time. A good screen sorts by fact (ownership, behavior); a bad screen telegraphs who you want, and professional survey-takers will happily become whoever that is.
3. **Awareness before exposure.** If the study measures recall, ask unaided (open-ended) before any brand or concept is shown — a shown list destroys unaided recall permanently.
4. **Concept and attitude questions.** Present the stimulus, then measure reactions on labeled scales. Scaled interest questions beat flat yes/no items because they capture intensity — and intensity is what forecasts behavior.
5. **Behavior and pricing.**
6. **Demographics last** — they feel intrusive, so they go where abandonment costs least.

**Wording discipline — the recurring sins:**

- **Leading:** any wording that praises, presumes, or pressures (stunning, unbeatable, revolutionary) manufactures the answer it wants.
- **Double-barreled:** two asks fused into one item; the answer is uninterpretable.
- **Vague:** unanchored words (often, regularly, pretty good) mean different things to different respondents.

**Scale discipline.** Five or seven points, endpoints labeled, direction consistent. When price matters, say the price — interest in an unpriced concept is interest in a fantasy.

**Keep it lean.** Every question costs completion rate. If it doesn't map to a decision the client must make, it doesn't ship.

guides.title: Sample Size, Margin of Error, and the z-Table
guides.body:
**What you're buying with a sample size is precision.** The margin of error (e) is the half-width of the confidence interval around any percentage the survey reports; the confidence level says how often intervals built this way capture the truth. Higher confidence or tighter margins cost more respondents — the client picks the trade-off, the analyst prices it.

**Step 1 — base sample size (large population):**

n0 = z² · p(1−p) / e²

- **z** comes from the confidence level:

| Confidence level | z |
|---|---|
| 80% | 1.28 |
| 90% | 1.645 |
| 95% | 1.96 |
| 99% | 2.58 |

- **p** is the expected proportion. When unknown, use **p = 0.5** — it maximizes p(1−p), so the estimate is conservative (never too small).
- **e** is the margin of error **as a decimal**: ±3% → 0.03, ±2.5% → 0.025. Forgetting the decimal conversion is the single most common way to be off by orders of magnitude.

**Step 2 — finite-population correction (FPC).** The base formula assumes an effectively infinite population. When the population size N is known and finite, correct:

n = n0 / (1 + (n0 − 1) / N)

The correction shrinks the requirement — meaningfully when n0 is large relative to N, only slightly when N is huge. Skipping it when N is known means quoting the client a bigger (more expensive) sample than the precision requires.

**Step 3 — round up.** Sample sizes are whole respondents, and rounding down would deliver less precision than promised. Always round up to the next whole respondent.

**Sanity checks before you hand numbers to anyone:** tighter margin → larger n (halving e roughly quadruples n0); higher confidence → larger n; the FPC should always make n smaller than n0, never larger.

resources.title: SoCal Housing & Lot-Use Atlas (extract)
resources.body:
**SoCal Housing & Lot-Use Atlas — 2025 edition (extract)**

*Table 14: Owner-occupied single-family housing stock by lot characteristics, six-county Southern California region (Los Angeles, Orange, San Diego, Riverside, San Bernardino, Ventura).*

Applying the study's qualification screen — owner-occupied single-family homes with usable yard space of at least 200 sq ft of level, accessible lot area; head of household aged 30–65; household income of $75,000 or more — the atlas estimates:

**N = 300,000 qualified households** in the six-county region.

Methodology note: estimates combine county assessor lot records, census household-income distributions, and aerial lot-coverage analysis. Figures are rounded to the nearest 10,000 households and reflect the most recent assessment year. This is the target-population figure to use for any finite-population sampling calculation in the Neo Smart Living engagement.

resources.title: Secondary-research recap (from our Round 4 analysis)
resources.body:
**Condensed summaries — the three articles analyzed in the secondary-research phase.**

**Article 1 — Market landscape.** The North American prefab backyard-structure market splits into four tiers. Mid-market leaders by estimated revenue: StudioPod Co. ($19M), YardHaus ($14M), ModuSpace ($11M) — the tier closest to the Tahoe Mini's positioning. Above them, Casita Collective ($8M, permitted ADUs with plumbing) and luxury-niche Tropez Outdoor ($3M, spa units); below, budget players ZenShed ($6M) and BackyardBox ($4M, storage-grade shells).

**Article 2 — Pricing benchmarks.** Across the mid-market tier, prevailing prices average roughly **$12,000 for compact units (~100 sq ft), $18,000 for standard (~120 sq ft), and $24,000 for deluxe (~160 sq ft)**. The Tahoe Mini's $23,000 sits near the top of the standard-size range — closer to deluxe pricing than to its size peers.

**Article 3 — Demand drivers.** Category growth tracks remote and hybrid work, home-wellness spending, and interest in permit-light structures that avoid full ADU approval timelines. Buyers cluster among owner-occupied single-family homeowners with usable yards — the same profile as Neo's target market.

resources.title: Focus-group findings summary
resources.body:
**Neo Smart Living — focus-group phase, key findings (moderator's summary).**

Across the groups, three themes dominated. **Privacy:** participants admired the floor-to-ceiling glass but repeatedly asked what the neighbors would see; several wanted privacy panels or frosted options before they would consider working — let alone exercising — inside. **Climate comfort:** many doubted a glass-walled unit would stay usable in Southern California heat and asked pointedly about insulation and cooling. **Price sensitivity:** the $23,000 figure met consistent resistance; participants anchored their acceptable prices a few thousand dollars below current list prices across every size tier discussed. Enthusiasm concentrated on two uses — a quiet home office and a wellness or hobby studio — with guest space a distant third. Several participants raised HOA approval and permit questions the survey should quantify. These themes shaped the concept, pricing, and open-ended questions in the quantitative instrument.
